To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority of epidermal tumour samples analysed by flow cytometric analysis show evidence for clonal heterogeneity, and this correlates with histological features of the sample.

(a) flow cytometry analysis of curetted epidermal cancers revealed a significant number of samples with DNA frequency distributions suggesting more than one stem‐cell population; (b) this finding was more common in the samples with squamoid differentiation (AK, BCC and SCC) than in the pure BCC; (c) the frequency distribution of DNA content was not related to the histological grade of differentiation; (d) the frequency distribution was not related to histological grade of

“The majority of human epidermal cancer curetted samples show clonal heterogeneity, as assessed by DNA frequency distributions obtained by flow cytometry, and the proportion of samples with clonal heterogeneity correlates with the degree of squamous cell differentiation.”
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of clonal heterogeneity and its relationship with histological features in curetted epidermal tumour samples.
the study of clonal heterogeneity in human epidermal tumors by flow cytometry.
the development of a method for the determination of the distribution of the DNA content in the nuclei of cells in a suspension.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the majority of epidermal tumour samples analysed showed features suggestive of the presence of more than one cell stem population, but that the frequency of such samples was significantly higher in those with squamous cell than in those with BCC differentiation.
the majority of BCCs, as well as some of the AKs, BOs and SCCs analysed in this study, are monoclonal.
the presence of more than one DNA stem cell population is more frequent in epidermal tumour samples with squamous than with basal cell differentiation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of BCCs (77%) and the majority of squamous cell carcinogenic lesions (AK, BO, SCC, BSC, 86%) have a clonal origin, but the latter are more heterogeneous.

the more the epidermal cancer or precancer has a squamous component (AK, BO, SCC, BSC), the more likely the sample has more than one stem population, and the less the epidermal tumor has a squamous cell component (BCC), the less likely the sample will have more than one stem line.
the majority (70%) of epidermal tumour samples with squamous differentiation have a heterogeneous DNA frequency distribution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a significant amount of heterogeneity in the epidermal tumors we studied.
there are many different types of cancer stem cell in a single tumor and they are not all the same.
the use of a single‐cell approach is essential for understanding the heterogeneity in the epidermal tumour cells.
